data.title: Bloomberg: Has Bitcoin truly matured after being accepted by Wall Street?
data.description:
Author: Teresa Xie, Bloomberg reporter; Translator: Jia Huan, ChainCatcher

Bitcoin is entering adulthood. At least in terms of age, it certainly is.

18 years ago, a person using the pseudonym Satoshi Nakamoto published a white paper envisioning a decentralized electronic payment system. This earliest form of cryptocurrency aimed to allow people to transfer money directly to each other without relying on banks or any central authority.

Now, Bitcoin will celebrate its 18th birthday this Saturday, and it's time to look back at how far it has come from Satoshi Nakamoto's original rebellious experiment. Many are familiar with this journey: some have made fortunes from it, others have had their relationships ruined; ecosystems have sprung up around it, and others have ultimately collapsed. Governments have bought it, celebrities have called it "rat poison," and many have debated its exact nature for years.

Along the way, Bitcoin has been declared dead and resurrected time and again; it has been rejected by the masses, but later gained a diverse range of supporters, including Wall Street.

This raises a crucial question: nearly 20 years after its inception, has Bitcoin truly matured, or is it merely feigning maturity? Wall Street Becomes a Supporter of Bitcoin "It has indeed come a long way," says Anastasia Melachrinos, Head of Growth at Kaiko. "Think about where Bitcoin first appeared—the dark web and forums. And in 18 years, we've gone from there to a completely new asset class." Bitcoin has made some unexpected friends and gained social acceptance, especially in recent years. Today, investors can invest in Bitcoin in various ways, including through products offered by Wall Street giants like BlackRock. BlackRock manages a $66 billion Bitcoin ETF (exchange-traded fund). Dozens of publicly traded companies have Bitcoin reserves on their balance sheets, and some of the world's wealthiest investors continue to praise it. The irony is clear. Bitcoin was originally created to challenge centralized finance; now, the very institutions it once sought to disrupt have become some of the strongest supporters of blockchain technology. Wall Street is accelerating its deployment of stablecoins, asset tokenization, and blockchain-based financial infrastructure, increasingly incorporating the technology into the financial system that Bitcoin initially attempted to bypass. There are many other examples, but few still evoke the idea of ​​rebelling against the traditional financial order. "Bitcoin's most fundamental significance lies in proving that value transfer can be completed without intermediaries," said Linda Jeng, Chief Legal and Policy Officer at Aave Labs. "Since then, Bitcoin has driven several rounds of development in digital finance. Technologies that were once on the fringes are becoming the new financial system." Volatility Declines, Price Movement Still Closely Follows US Stocks Looking at stability, Bitcoin has indeed made some progress in this area. The increasing popularity of ETFs has made investing in Bitcoin more convenient, which has contributed to a significant reduction in its previously dramatic price fluctuations. Earlier this month, its 30-day volatility fell to its lowest level in three years.

Chart caption: Bitcoin volatility declines, with its 30-day volatility falling to its lowest level in three years earlier this month. Source: Bloomberg.

This doesn't mean Bitcoin has completely shed its immature aspects; it still experiences significant ups and downs. Last October, a sudden sell-off resulted in the liquidation of a record $19 billion in leveraged positions in a single day, and this is far from the first time the crypto industry has experienced a boom-and-bust cycle.

This doesn't mean Bitcoin has completely shed its immature aspects; it still experiences significant volatility. Last October, a sudden sell-off led to the liquidation of a record $19 billion in leveraged positions in a single day, and this is far from the first time the crypto industry has experienced such a dramatic rise and fall.

Then there was the crypto winter of 2022, when in November, FTX, the crypto exchange founded by Sam Bankman-Fried, collapsed, wiping out over $2 trillion in market capitalization from crypto assets. Moreover, Bitcoin's price movements still mirror those of the US stock market. For example, it is highly correlated with the Nasdaq 100 index, indicating a lack of independence in its price movements. On its 18th birthday, the market lacked a celebratory atmosphere. As Bitcoin matured, it also lost some of its edge. It is no longer a rebel challenging tradition in the financial markets, nor a bold bet in the eyes of risk-takers, but rather an asset that ordinary investors would include in a balanced portfolio. Just last week, venture capital giant Andreessen Horowitz officially changed the name of its crypto fund from a16z Crypto to a16z Frontier. On the eve of Bitcoin's birthday, the market lacked much of a celebratory atmosphere. Based on current trends, this month may be Bitcoin's worst month since June. The upward momentum accumulated over the summer failed to continue, and the price is now hovering around $80,000. Supporters believe Bitcoin will soon return to $100,000, and may even eventually reach $1 million; critics, however, argue it's worthless. Anthony Scaramucci, founder of Skybridge Capital, first bought Bitcoin at $6,000 years ago and later at $16,000. He stated that he has always viewed this investment as a five-year bet. He predicts Bitcoin will double in the next five years, which, according to his calculations, equates to a compound annual return of approximately 15%. "Bitcoin is the benchmark of this industry," he said in an interview. "It will still exist long after you and I are gone."

data.title: Chainalysis: Sub-Saharan Africa Becomes the Fastest Growing Region for Crypto
data.description:
Author: Chainalysis; Translator: Luffy, Foresight News

Chainalysis, a data research institution in the crypto field, released its latest Global Crypto Adoption Report. The report's sub-Saharan Africa section mentions that the region's crypto economy grew by 13.4% year-on-year to $101 billion, the fastest growth rate globally. South Africa and Nigeria are the two core markets, experiencing a surge in demand for stablecoins, and the proportion of self-custodied wallets in the region is the highest globally. The local crypto adoption is mainly driven by real financial needs such as cross-border remittances and daily payments; the future market trend largely depends on regulatory clarity.

While sub-Saharan Africa is the smallest region in terms of global crypto economy size, it is also the fastest growing.

During the statistical period from July 1, 2025 to June 30, 2026, the region's cryptocurrency market grew by 13.4%, reaching $101 billion, with South Africa being the core driver of this growth. A very real reason behind the local cryptocurrency adoption is that many individuals and businesses still struggle to access affordable and reliable financial services. For ordinary people, cryptocurrency offers an alternative for managing funds and cross-border transfers; for businesses, it enables faster and lower-cost cross-border payments and settlements. In this region, the appeal of cryptocurrency lies not in creating entirely new financial products or speculative investment channels, but in addressing real-world financial pain points. As Mercy Emmanuel, Head of Stablecoin and Blockchain Business at Nigerian fintech company Flutterwave, stated, "For the African market, commercially viable innovations should simplify the frictions of existing financial activities, rather than deliberately increasing business complexity in order to use blockchain." South Africa and Nigeria dominate the regional market. South Africa and Nigeria dominate the sub-Saharan African crypto market, together accounting for more than three-quarters of the region's total crypto trading volume.

South Africa is the largest crypto economy in sub-Saharan Africa

However, the development paths of the two countries have clearly diverged. During the reporting period, South Africa's crypto economy reached $39.3 billion, a year-on-year increase of 52%, bucking the trend in a global bear market. Growth covered all statistical sectors, with the core drivers being cross-border P2P stablecoin transfers and fund flows related to various crypto services.

Nigeria's crypto market size is similar to South Africa's, reaching $38.1 billion, but transaction volume declined by 3% year-on-year.

The growth in centralized exchanges (CEXs) and the crypto services sector was offset by a 45% drop in decentralized exchange (DEX) trading volume and a 17% decline in cross-border P2P trading volume. Meanwhile, Nigeria ranked third globally in Chainalysis's grassroots crypto adoption index. South Africa and Nigeria account for three-quarters of the total crypto economy in sub-Saharan Africa. Looking at other countries, the trading activity of CEXs and DEXs profoundly impacts growth curves in various regions. Ghana's crypto market grew by 80% to $5.1 billion, with both CEX and DEX trading rising in tandem; Senegal's crypto trading volume surged 215% to $2.3 billion, with all growth coming from centralized exchanges. Conversely, Ethiopia's crypto market declined by 8% to $3.7 billion, primarily due to a contraction in DEX trading. These divergences illustrate the uneven pace of crypto adoption within the region. Smaller markets offer significant growth potential and can scale rapidly, but they also experience greater volatility and are highly susceptible to market fluctuations and regulatory changes. Regulation and market conditions can either accelerate adoption or directly disrupt growth momentum. Research shows that personal wallets account for a very high percentage of crypto funds in sub-Saharan Africa's crypto market, reflecting the unique adoption model there: individuals are the core holders and transferrs of crypto assets. During the statistical period, funds received by personal wallets accounted for 32.3% of the total amount received in the region, the highest proportion globally. This indicates that local users choose cryptocurrency largely for self-management of their funds, rather than relying on custodian intermediaries such as exchanges. Cross-border P2P transfers constituted the majority of these funds, accounting for 70.9% of the total amount received by personal wallets; domestic P2P transactions accounted for 18.5%; and transfers from crypto service platforms to personal wallets accounted for 10.7%.

One-third of crypto funds in sub-Saharan Africa flow to personal self-custodial wallets

Insufficient supply of custody services and regulatory uncertainty are important reasons why users prefer self-custodial wallets. Take Nigeria as an example: From 2021 to 2023, the Central Bank of Nigeria prohibited banks from providing services to crypto exchanges, and subsequently, the country also had tax disputes with leading international crypto platforms. These regulatory changes lead users to favor self-custodial services to avoid the risks brought about by future policy changes and market shutdowns.

Insufficient supply of custody services and regulatory uncertainty are important reasons why users prefer self-custodial wallets. For example, in Nigeria: From 2021 to 2023, the Central Bank of Nigeria prohibited banks from providing services to crypto exchanges, and subsequently, the country also had tax disputes with leading international crypto platforms. These regulatory changes make users inclined to self-custody, avoiding the risks brought about by future policy changes and market shutdowns.

Stablecoin trading volume in the region has increased sixfold, while Bitcoin inflows have shrunk by 60%. Stablecoins are rapidly defining the sub-Saharan African crypto market landscape. From 2022 to 2026, the amount of stablecoins received through P2P channels increased sixfold, from $2.3 billion to $14.6 billion; during the same period, Bitcoin inflows fell by 60%, from $36 billion to $14.6 billion.

Stablecoin trading volume increased sixfold, Bitcoin fell 60%

This change highlights the practical value of stablecoins: local individuals and businesses can use stablecoins to hold the value of foreign currencies such as the US dollar without opening foreign currency bank accounts. In sub-Saharan Africa, where local currencies are highly volatile, foreign exchange access is limited, and cross-border transfers are expensive and slow, stablecoins can be used for receiving payments, preserving value, and transferring funds across regions.

The application scenarios of stablecoins have gone beyond the scope of transactions and have attracted widespread attention.

Philip Kwaw Sebuabe, head of the virtual assets department at the Central Bank of Ghana, stated, "The appeal of stablecoins extends beyond trading; cross-border payments, remittance settlements, and foreign currency asset preservation are core applications." Gillian Darko, Vice President of Strategy at Yellowcard.io, a stablecoin payment infrastructure service provider, shares this view, believing stablecoins represent the region's biggest opportunity in the coming year. Stablecoins can meet the market's demand for reliable payment systems, bridging the gap between payments, savings, and investment. Cross-border remittances best illustrate the value of stablecoins: regional stablecoin remittances doubled year-on-year, increasing from $235 million to $492 million; Bitcoin remittances remained largely unchanged. The nearly fivefold increase in the number of stablecoin cross-border transfers indicates a rise in genuine demand, not just a paper increase driven by rising asset prices. Stablecoins are replacing Bitcoin as the mainstream crypto remittance asset. This is driven by Africa's strong demand for cross-border financial connectivity. Mercy Emmanuel of Flutterwave noted, "Africa has a strong demand for international financial connectivity, but payment links are fragmented by different currencies, markets, and financial institutions. Stablecoins have the opportunity to bridge the value gap between these isolated systems." Against this backdrop, local currency stablecoins are gaining attention. Rob Downes, Head of Digital Assets at Absa CIB, a pan-African bank, pointed out that local currency stablecoins are emerging, with pilot programs in South Africa, Ghana, Kenya, and Tanzania. For example, the Central Bank of Ghana is studying a cedi-backed stablecoin scheme: the stablecoin handles settlement, and the recipient can ultimately receive Ghanaian cedi through a bank account or mobile wallet, without needing to hold the crypto assets themselves. Philip Kwaw Sebuabe also mentioned another major advantage of stablecoins: they are not restricted by traditional bank operating hours. Bank transfers are typically limited by weekdays, weekends, and holidays, while stablecoin transactions can be settled 24/7, which is particularly important for international trade, cross-border remittances, and financial markets. These trends illustrate that stablecoins fulfill two major functions: providing exposure to foreign currencies such as the US dollar, while simultaneously optimizing regional payment systems. The large-scale adoption of stablecoins largely depends on clear regulation. Ghana and Kenya have already introduced stablecoin-related regulations last year, setting rules for the rapidly expanding stablecoin market and supporting wider adoption. Intra-African Encrypted Payment Channels Expand as Businesses Seek Low-Cost Cross-Border Settlement

Research observes rapid growth in business-to-business payments within Africa, with cryptocurrencies playing an increasingly important role in cross-border transfers between businesses in the region. The statistics include payments from consumers to merchants and transfers between businesses.

This growth stems from long-standing pain points in traditional African cross-border commercial payments: only a small portion of intra-African cross-border payments are cleared within Africa, leading to high losses and regulatory friction. Against this backdrop, encrypted payment channels connecting African merchants and consumers have become a highly attractive alternative.

Data shows that during the statistical period, the number of active encrypted payment channels in the region nearly doubled, from 80 to 152, with 95 channels experiencing two-way fund flows; the total transaction volume more than doubled, from $34.3 million to $116.5 million.

The average transaction size per channel increased from $429,000 to $766,000, indicating broader regional financial connectivity and continued deepening of transaction activity. The number of intra-Saharan African cross-border commercial payment channels has nearly doubled. This trend signifies not only a shift in crypto-based fund flows between African markets, but also that crypto payment channels are serving merchants and consumers underserved by traditional financial infrastructure. While regional demand for these crypto payment channels is strong, the ability of financial institutions and mainstream payment service providers to accept cryptocurrencies will determine the sustainability of this sector's growth. Gillian Darko emphasized the role of banks in intra-African transfers, international payments, and remittances; for stablecoin payments to become widespread, they must be integrated with the existing banking system, allowing on-chain transactions to access a broader range of financial infrastructure. North America is the main source of crypto remittances to Sub-Saharan Africa. Besides corporate payments, crypto remittances are gaining increasing importance in Sub-Saharan Africa. Traditional remittances are expensive, making cryptocurrencies a highly attractive low-cost alternative. Remittances are a significant source of income for many countries in the region; in countries like Gambia and Lesotho, remittances account for a high percentage of GDP. In 2025, Sub-Saharan Africa received a large amount of cross-border remittances. However, the cost of remittances to the region remains persistently high: World Bank data shows that the average fee for a $200 remittance is among the highest globally. For recipients, even a slight decrease in transaction fees can bring tangible benefits. Encrypted remittances play a crucial role in this scenario, reducing costs, breaking down barriers, and accelerating transfers. Research shows that developed countries are the main recipients of encrypted remittances to sub-Saharan Africa, with a total amount of $888 million during the statistical period, a year-on-year increase of 36%. The number of transactions is growing even faster, increasing by 43%, and is expected to exceed 1 million transactions in 2026.

The total amount of encrypted remittances from Western countries to sub-Saharan Africa continues to rise

North America, with its large populations of Nigerians, Ghanaians, and Ethiopians, is the largest source of encrypted remittances, amounting to $645 million. Australia and New Zealand saw the fastest growth, with remittances increasing from $48 million to $143 million, nearly tripling; Western Europe saw a moderate increase, from $79 million to $100 million.

The total amount of encrypted remittances from Western countries to sub-Saharan Africa continues to rise

North America, with its large populations of Nigerians, Ghanaians, and Ethiopians, is the largest source of encrypted remittances, amounting to $645 million.

The scale of cryptocurrency remittances is strongly correlated with the number of African immigrants in the country

In terms of per capita outflow, Canada ranks first: the cryptocurrency remittances per sub-Saharan African immigrant rose from $586 to $736; the US saw an increase to $143; and Western Europe saw only a rise from $14.5 to $17.9.

...

Canada has the highest average remittance amount, while Western Europe is generally lower

The differences are the result of the combined effects of the economic and policy environment of the remittance source country, the income level of the expatriates, and the maturity of the local cryptocurrency market. Job opportunities and social welfare affect the amount of funds that expatriates can transfer; the degree of cryptocurrency adoption determines whether people choose cryptocurrency remittances.

North America has a high proportion of cryptocurrency remittances precisely because of the large number of African immigrants there and the maturity of the cryptocurrency market. This also shows that the correlation between immigration and cryptocurrency remittances is highly dependent on the local environment of the immigrant's country of settlement.

South African businesses are widely accepting crypto payments. Research has found that South Africa has developed a sizable crypto-based economy, with consumers and merchants directly using cryptocurrencies to purchase goods and services. The research uses merchant-facing payment data within South Africa: wallet-to-wallet transfers where the recipient's transaction characteristics are merchant service payments. The scope is broad, including businesses using crypto payments for long-term service contracts and consumers scanning QR codes to buy fast food. To exclude extreme large transactions, a single transaction limit of $50,000 was set. This category includes legitimate merchants, P2P traders, and other sellers. During the statistical period, the transaction volume of such merchant payments in South Africa reached $8.34 billion, showing a continuous quarter-on-quarter increase. In the second quarter of 2026 (the last quarter of the statistical period), service-related transfers exceeded $1 billion more than in the third quarter of 2025 (the starting quarter of the statistical period). The growth rate of these merchant payments even exceeds the rapid growth of institutional crypto fund inflows in South Africa, which totaled $1.29 billion during the same period. The growth rate of service-related payments has already surpassed institutional platform fund inflows. The growth of merchant payments is based on the continuous improvement of South Africa's crypto payment infrastructure. In 2025, the mainstream QR code payment service Scan to Pay and the crypto platform MoneyBadger launched a cooperative payment solution, allowing consumers to use Bitcoin at over 600,000 offline stores. As of August 2026, this partnership covered a large number of retail locations. MoneyBadger CEO Carel van Wyk stated that South African users are increasingly using cryptocurrency for everyday purchases, both in-store and online. The company's Q2 2026 payment data analysis shows that half of transactions were under $13, and 87% were under $60; e-commerce transactions accounted for 48% of total payments. "Combined with our observed repurchase data, this indicates that cryptocurrency is integrating into the daily consumption habits of locals." South Africa: A Crypto Hub in Sub-Saharan Africa South Africa has long been a gateway for international investment in Africa, boasting the Johannesburg Stock Exchange, a mature banking system, a complete industrial sector, and stable trade links across Africa, supporting the flow of physical capital throughout the continent. Chainalysis data shows that South Africa is also a hub for cross-border cryptocurrency fund flows in Africa. To verify whether the flow of crypto funds from South Africa matches traditional economic and trade relations, the team compared the flow of crypto cross-border payments and foreign direct investment (FDI) from South Africa: South Africa has long been a core source of FDI within Africa. Crypto funds flowing from South Africa to Nigeria, Kenya, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Tanzania, Namibia, and Zimbabwe highly overlap with traditional FDI flows, indicating that there is some overlap between crypto fund channels and traditional investment channels, relying on established commercial and economic relations.

South Africa's Crypto Payment and Investment Landscape in the African Region

However, the overlap is not entirely consistent. Botswana and Zambia receive large amounts of FDI from South Africa, but relatively little crypto funds from South Africa; Senegal and Cameroon are the opposite. This indicates that the flow of crypto funds is only partially related to traditional outward investment.

Even if crypto funds do not completely follow FDI, the overlap in several core markets proves that South Africa is becoming a hub for regional crypto commerce and transactions. This is corroborated by the conclusion of rapid growth in payments by South African local merchants: the weight of crypto in South African business activities continues to increase.

However, South Africa's hub status may change in the future. In August 2026, the South African Treasury and the South African Reserve Bank (SARB) released a draft "Guidance Manual for Cross-Border Crypto Assets," planning to incorporate crypto assets into the country's capital flow management framework. The draft originally stipulated that individuals could only transfer crypto assets overseas through authorized local service providers; businesses were prohibited from two-way cross-border transfers of crypto assets. The draft sparked strong opposition, and the South African Reserve Bank recently stated that it is revising the new regulations, eliminating the prior approval requirement. Regardless of the final version, these rules will profoundly affect the cross-border flow of crypto assets for individuals and businesses. Nigeria: Rapid Rise of Local Crypto Services, Local Exchanges Dominate Growth Nigeria is the region's second-largest crypto economy, with a market highly biased towards crypto services. A significant amount of funds flowed to crypto platforms and various services. During the statistical period, Nigerian users transferred $25.2 billion to crypto service platforms, a 172% increase compared to four years ago, exceeding the regional average growth rate. The growth in Nigeria's service sector fund inflows outpaced other sub-Saharan African countries. Almost all of the increase came from domestic exchanges, contributing $4.13 billion, accounting for 92% of the total increase. Overall, domestic platforms received $6.22 billion, representing half of the total inflows to Nigerian centralized exchanges. A dramatic shift in market share: Nigerian exchanges accounted for 27% of the market in 2025, compared to only 7% in 2022. This change stems from Nigeria's restrictive policies on international exchanges in recent years. In 2024, regulators, concerned about the devaluation of the naira and the increased exchange rate volatility caused by cryptocurrencies, temporarily restricted user access to international platforms such as Binance, Kraken, and Coinbase. Although the restrictions were temporary, ongoing disagreements between regulators and leading international exchanges have reduced the number of platforms available for Nigerian users to trade naira pairs, creating a window of opportunity for domestic exchanges to grow. The continuously improving regulatory framework is further boosting the local ecosystem. In July 2026, the Nigerian President signed an executive order for the harmonization of virtual assets, establishing an inter-agency coordination committee led by the central bank to unify the regulation of virtual assets, including stablecoins. A controlled sandbox environment was also established to test new products. Looking ahead, the Nigerian SEC has already released draft rules for the operation, custody, and market of virtual assets, requiring exchanges and custodians to meet higher capital requirements by June 2027. This policy is expected to further strengthen the Nigerian crypto ecosystem, providing local platforms with a clear regulatory framework and expanding their service boundaries. However, the increased capital and compliance costs will benefit large, well-funded institutions, reshaping the market competition landscape. P2P transactions remain important in the Nigerian market; the proportion of Bitcoin in small-amount transfers is far higher than in other regions and the global average, a unique characteristic of the Nigerian crypto market. During the statistical period, Bitcoin accounted for 92% of small-value wallet transfers under $10,000 in Nigeria, amounting to $923 million (out of a total of $1 billion); in other parts of sub-Saharan Africa, this proportion was only 22%. This indicates that Bitcoin is the core medium for daily peer-to-peer small-value transfers in Nigeria, unlike other markets where stablecoins are dominant. Overall, the Nigerian market is characterized by the continued expansion of its local exchange ecosystem and a high reliance on Bitcoin for small-scale P2P transactions. Even with the continued development of formal crypto services, local demand for crypto remains driven by users' need for direct and flexible value transfer. As local services and regulations mature, understanding this unique user habit is crucial for predicting the future of the Nigerian market. Looking ahead, the differentiated crypto adoption paths in sub-Saharan Africa are worth monitoring over the next year: the South African crypto market is increasingly geared towards commercial payments, while the Nigerian market is characterized by P2P transactions and small-scale Bitcoin transfers. Across the region, the continued demand for cross-border payment settlements is driving crypto adoption, and financial institutions are gradually entering the market. Stablecoins are breaking down payment barriers and currency barriers. Future trends depend on multiple factors, including capital investment and user demand, with regulation being a decisive variable. Clearer regulations can give businesses, investors, and financial institutions confidence to participate in crypto, accelerating its adoption. As Rob Downes of Absa CIB stated, "At this stage, regulation is undoubtedly the most crucial driving force for the development of crypto in Africa." The core issue lies in whether the capital continuously flowing into the crypto sector in sub-Saharan Africa can be transformed into regional financial connectivity and inclusive financial services. In the long run, the value of cryptocurrencies in Africa depends on whether they can consistently generate real benefits for individuals and businesses, moving beyond mere hype and experimentation to truly become a functional part of regional financial and commercial infrastructure.

data.title: The most pressing bottleneck for AI today: cheap funding is drying up.
data.description:
Author: Gao Zhimou, Wall Street Insights

Confidence supports financing, and financing supports investment; once confidence weakens, the contraction of funds will in turn damage investment and growth expectations.

In the past few years, AI companies have easily raised hundreds of billions of dollars, with Wall Street vying to invest and rarely interfering, focusing on "plenty of money and little trouble." Now, lenders and investors are becoming more selective, and the terms are becoming increasingly stringent.

This week, the two most sought-after leading players in the AI ​​industry have both encountered setbacks in the capital market: Blackstone told investors that Anthropic may only receive a junk rating after its IPO; OpenAI cut its new round of financing target from $30 billion to about $20 billion.

Both things point to the same change: for the US AI industry, cheap money is becoming increasingly difficult to obtain.

Dan Ivascyn, Chief Investment Officer of Pacific Investment Management Company (Pimco), stated: "The bar for proving to lenders that these investments can generate sufficient revenue is getting higher and higher...weak links will be the first to be hit." The money is still there, but it's now a buyer's market. Since its inception, ChatGPT has seen AI companies utilize almost every source of funding, including venture capital, stocks, banks, bonds, and private credit. According to Bank of America, AI-related corporate bond issuance in the US market is projected to reach $394 billion in 2025, and has already reached $655 billion as of mid-October this year. Analysts predict it will approach $1 trillion next year. The demand for funding is increasing, but lenders are becoming increasingly hesitant. Investors have three main concerns: growing resistance to data centers in various regions could delay large-scale projects; AI profits from hyperscale cloud providers and startups like Anthropic and OpenAI may not materialize as quickly as promised; and the surge in stock and bond issuances has led to excessive investor exposure to AI. New trading conditions are evident in every corner of the market. Bonds from large tech companies like SpaceX and Meta are trading at significant discounts; AI cloud companies like CoreWeave, Nebius, and Nscale, which rely on debt to build computing power, have effectively been shut out of the bond market in recent weeks; even powerful companies like Broadcom have had to offer more favorable terms to banks to secure loans. Anthropic is the latest example. It plans to raise up to $100 billion in its mid-November IPO and states in its prospectus that it will invest over $800 billion in computing infrastructure by 2045. According to the Financial Times, Blackstone recently told investors that, based on guidance from major rating agencies, Anthropic is more likely to receive a BB- ​​or higher rating after its IPO, whereas Blackstone had previously expected it to achieve an investment-grade rating by the end of the year. According to S&P and Fitch's system, BBB- and above are investment grade, while BB+ and below are speculative grade, commonly known as "junk" debt. Many insurance companies and pension funds are restricted from holding large amounts of junk debt; a rating in this range means that Anthropic's access to financing will be narrower and more expensive. The $63 billion chip leasing deal between Broadcom and Anthropic reached this week was also negotiated under tense circumstances. According to the Wall Street Journal, Broadcom CEO Hock Tan personally intervened in the negotiations at the last minute to stabilize the banks' sentiment; over $42 billion of the senior loans in the deal were guaranteed by Broadcom's high A-grade rating. Anthropic also listed the financing constraints of power suppliers as a risk factor in its prospectus: even if it can raise funds itself, it worries about whether its suppliers can. OpenAI faces a similar situation. According to the Financial Times, it has reduced its fundraising target to approximately $20 billion, lowering its valuation from $1.4 trillion to $1.25 trillion; the Wall Street Journal, citing sources familiar with the matter, reported that OpenAI has raised less than half of its initial $30 billion target to date. Some investors have reduced their subscription amounts, while others want to wait until Anthropic goes public before making a decision. While reputable leading companies can still secure funding, market patience is waning. This week, AI-related stocks and bonds were sold off as tech companies delivered disappointing earnings reports: Alphabet's market capitalization evaporated by approximately $500 billion on Thursday, the largest single-day drop in history; Intel plunged 29% on Friday; and the Nasdaq Composite Index fell 2.9% on Friday, marking one of the largest sell-offs in US stocks since the AI ​​boom began. If the volatility continues, financing will only become more difficult. New cloud providers: the first to be shut out. The pressure will first fall on the weakest links in the credit chain. One of the most active issuers in the AI ​​debt market is companies known as "neocloud." They own or lease data centers, deploy AI servers, and then sell the computing power to large tech companies, trading firms, and AI startups. Many new cloud vendors, transitioning from cryptocurrency mining companies, have little experience operating AI infrastructure. Their borrowing costs were already high before the market turmoil, making them highly sensitive to rising interest rates. The turning point came in September. The Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time in three years; Oracle notified the developer of a large data center in New Mexico of a delay in starting full rent payments due to power supply and approval issues, prompting lenders across the country to reassess the construction risks of their projects. CoreWeave's bonds, issued earlier this year with a coupon rate of 9.75%, now yield over 15% in the secondary market. The decline in bond prices and the rise in yields indicate a significant increase in its borrowing costs in the short term. Bankers have warned in recent weeks that the high-yield bond market for new cloud vendors is essentially closed to new issuances, with yields above 15% being unaffordable for borrowers. Nebius has sold approximately $2.7 billion in stock to investors such as Nvidia and issued billions of dollars in convertible bonds since 2024, but its funding needs remain unmet. It had initially considered issuing its first high-yield bond but ultimately abandoned the plan, opting instead to collect upfront payments from customers. CEO Arkady Volozh stated in Berlin last week that some funding sources, such as asset-backed securities and the bond market, "may be temporarily closed," but tools like customer upfront payments "are probably enough to allow us to build at least this 1 gigawatt of capacity." COO Ophir Nave stated that the asset-backed financing market remains open. Equity financing is also proving difficult. Sources familiar with the matter said that Lambda sought to raise $4 billion in its final pre-IPO funding round, but lowered its target valuation from $14.5 billion to $13 billion after investors such as Coatue decided not to participate. British cloud provider Nscale, which originally planned to list in November, is now leaning towards a December IPO. It is also negotiating with investors like Nvidia for funding for Anthropic's $45 billion data center in West Virginia, but the shift in the market and the demand for stricter terms have slowed its prospectus update. Some bankers have told Nscale that its IPO may not reach its previously set valuation of $30 billion to $35 billion. Giants: Even with high ratings, investors will "fill up." Meta, Amazon, Alphabet, and Microsoft are at the other end of the credit risk spectrum. They have top ratings and ample borrowing space on their balance sheets; the problem lies in the scale of their financing. This year, they have issued bonds aggressively in the high-grade bond market and have indicated they will continue to do so. Investment firms, insurance companies, and pension funds that provided loans are already feeling the pinch and are worried about over-concentration of holdings in the same sector. "The real question is, how much can investors really fit into one name, one theme?" Ivascyn said. On Friday, bond prices for several hyperscale cloud vendors fell to near record lows, with yields significantly higher than typical investment-grade corporate bonds. Despite their top ratings, they are already borrowing at a higher cost than typical investment-grade companies. Everyone wants to get ahead of the game. According to a Reuters analysis of LSEG consensus forecasts, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Oracle are projected to have capital expenditures exceeding their free cash flow by 2027, with approximately $1.57 of new capital expenditure for every $1 of additional operating cash flow. data.title: Anthropic is about to go public: Is large-scale modeling a good business?
data.description:
On October 26, 2026, Anthropic officially filed for an IPO with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, planning to list on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT. Media reports projected a valuation of $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion. Even before the bell rang, its value was already at least a trillion dollars. Regardless of its post-IPO performance, this day is likely to leave a mark on economic history. Anthropic is a significant bellwether in this intelligent revolution. Many people link the economic value of AI with the commercial value of model companies: since AI can change the world, leading model companies should be making a fortune, right? If Anthropic continues its upward trajectory, the market will have even more reason to believe that today's massive investment will eventually pay off. The story grew grander, and more money was invested. But if growth fell short of expectations, doubts would spread along the industry chain: if model companies weren't making money, how long could orders from cloud vendors, chipmakers, and data centers continue? A single company's performance thus influenced confidence in the entire technological revolution. But this connection also easily obscured a difference: the wealth created by AI might remain with large model companies, or it might flow to businesses and consumers using it through lower prices and higher efficiency. Anthropic's IPO presented us with two questions simultaneously: How much value can the intelligent revolution create? And how much value can one share by investing in a large model company? The answers to these two questions are not necessarily the same. We often say, "Great industries, mediocre investments." If we were to rank the greatest industries of the 20th century, electricity would certainly be at the head of the table. Electricity has transformed factories, cities, and the lives of ordinary people. But just because lights illuminate countless homes doesn't mean that everyone who invests in electricity will benefit. Around 1900, there were hundreds of electricity companies in the United States, most of which later failed due to market competition, debt crises, and the Great Depression. Among them, one notable name was Insall. He initially served as Edison's personal secretary, taking over the Chicago Edison Company in 1892. Through large-scale generators, grid-connected power supply, and low-price expansion, he turned electricity into a massive business. However, in 1932, his company went bankrupt due to excessive debt, leaving 600,000 shareholders with nothing. He fled to Greece but was extradited back to the United States for trial. The automotive industry, hailed as the crown jewel of the industrial age, has seen investors in auto stocks consistently profit. Warren Buffett once said he possessed a 70-page list of over 2,000 American automakers from that era. Sadly, nearly a century later, only General Motors, Ford, and Chrysler remain, and their long-term returns have been less than satisfactory. From 1956 to 2019, Ford's annualized return was 5.6%, which, if you bought into the leading company, was roughly equivalent to buying government bonds. General Motors even went into bankruptcy reorganization in 2009. Later, car production continued, but the old company's common stock was officially cancelled on March 31, 2011, with shareholders receiving no compensation. Changing the world and making shareholders money are two different things. Buffett's conclusion is: the key to investing is not judging the extent to which an industry will change society, but judging a company's competitive advantage and how long that advantage can be maintained. Reading Anthropic's prospectus, I always thought of these stories. "Intelligence will change the world" easily leads to the conclusion that "large-scale companies will make investors a lot of money." But there's a long way to go from the former to the latter. If we look at Buffett's stock-picking preferences, it can be summarized in one sentence: profits can grow continuously without requiring a proportional increase in new capital. His example is See's Candies. From its acquisition in 1972 to 2007, See's generated $1.35 billion in pre-tax profits, while only needing to invest an additional $32 million in operating capital to support business growth. The remaining money could be given to the parent company, paid taxes, and then reinvested in other businesses. Using this standard to measure Anthropic is clearly not suitable at present. However, it's not surprising that a rapidly expanding company at the forefront of technology would experience cash flow difficulties. The key question is: going forward, is it possible for it to become a business that consistently generates cash flow for shareholders? We can break this down into three parts: First, can training large models generate revenue? Second, how much more money needs to be invested annually to continue selling AI? Third, can the profits remain with the model company long-term? Three Questions About the Business Model of Large Models

First, can training large models make money?

First, can training large models be profitable?

Anthropic's business is quite simple: selling "intelligence" by token. Of its $16.286 billion revenue in the first half of 2026, approximately $13.1 billion (80%) came from usage-based billing; subscriptions such as Enterprise Edition and Pro/Max generated $3.2 billion (20%). Eighty percent is charged based on usage, and the remaining 20% ​​is charged via monthly or annual fees. This resembles a power company's bill, rather than a software or platform company's bill.

This business model has one advantage: once the same model is trained, serving the first customer and the 100 millionth customer doesn't require retraining. Inference still consumes computing power, but the initial R&D investment can be amortized by increased usage. As long as the increase in usage is enough to offset the price reduction, revenue can continue to grow; if the unit service cost decreases faster than the price, the gross margin will also increase. Anthropic's financial statements already show this change. Operating revenue increased from $41 million in 2023 to $386 million in 2024, and then jumped to $4.585 billion in 2025. By 2026, it had achieved $16.286 billion in revenue in the first half of the year alone. Since 2024, while revenue has expanded, gross margin has also improved rapidly: from -94.8% in 2024 to 39.5% in 2025, and further to 85.4% in the first half of 2026. In other words, for every $100 a customer paid in 2024, the company's corresponding operating cost was close to $195; by the first half of 2026, this cost had dropped to about $15. Compared to major Chinese model manufacturers, this figure is quite impressive. Zhipu and MiniMax's revenue is less than 1% of Anthropic's, and their gross profit margin is only around 20%. At least in terms of serving paying customers, Anthropic has crossed a significant threshold: customer payments significantly exceed current operating costs. However, a high gross profit margin does not necessarily mean the company is profitable. Large models are divided into training and inference phases. The $2.38 billion in operating costs mainly corresponds to the computing power and infrastructure used to serve customers during the inference phase of the trained models. The money spent on continuing to research and train the next generation of models is primarily recorded in R&D expenses and hasn't been deducted from the $85 gross profit. This leads to the second question—how much more money needs to be invested each year to continue selling intelligence? See's Candy doesn't require technological advancements; it doesn't need to invent a chocolate bar with twice the intelligence every year. Leading-edge model companies don't have that luxury. Customers buy Claude largely because of its capabilities. But competitors are constantly releasing new models, and customers' demands for accuracy, speed, price, and task completion are constantly increasing. The company must continue to invest to secure the foundation for the next round of revenue. How long can a cutting-edge model stay ahead? Currently, it seems to be only a few months. A telling figure in the prospectus is that from July to September 2026, over 80% of Anthropic's revenue came from model versions released between April and September of that year. The main driver of revenue is now the models released in the last six months. Previously, power plants were built, depreciated over 30-40 years, and then generated electricity revenue for decades. Now, large model companies rebuild an even larger power plant every year. The prospectus shows that in the first half of 2026, total computing power and infrastructure costs amounted to $8.945 billion. Of the 2.38 billion yuan recorded in operating costs and used to serve customers, only 6 billion yuan was used to train the next generation of models. In other words, for every 100 yuan spent on computing power, less than 30 yuan was used to sell tokens, and over 70 yuan was used to build the next model. Of course, continuous investment itself is not a sin. Buffett also invests in utilities that require substantial capital. The real dividing line is: does each additional investment yield a commensurate return? If R&D investment can open up a larger market, increase customer payments, and reduce service costs, then this money is a valuable investment. If the investment is increasing but mainly used to avoid being left behind by competitors, shareholders must ask: Is the company accumulating advantages or simply paying the price left at the table? What's more complicated is that these investments are no longer just R&D budgets that can be adjusted annually. Anthropic doesn't build its own data centers; its computing power is mainly leased from Amazon and Google. Therefore, its balance sheet doesn't show much factory or equipment; "capital expenditures" are hidden in operating costs and off-balance-sheet procurement commitments—in the first half of 2026, Anthropic's non-cancellable procurement commitments increased from approximately $54.6 billion at the end of 2025 to $265.6 billion at the end of June, a 4.9-fold increase in six months; projected lease payments for contracts signed but not yet leased increased from $50.2 billion to $321.4 billion. Subsequently, the company signed or revised a large number of infrastructure agreements. If subsequent commitments and conditional expenditures are included, the future expenditures involved reach trillions of dollars. These so-called non-cancellable procurement commitments, though not appearing on the balance sheet, are essentially a form of liability. For example, in Anthropic's agreements with Google and Amazon, as long as the supplier fulfills its obligations, the company is usually required to make up the agreed minimum expenditure even if the actual usage is insufficient. This creates a "short-term borrowing for long-term investment" type of maturity mismatch: the company promises suppliers fixed expenditures for many years, while customers promise monthly, fixed-amount revenue that can be discontinued at any time. Of the $13.1 billion in revenue generated in the first half of the year, not a single penny came from customer contracts with five-year terms. In the history of electricity, Insall failed precisely because of this. His power plants were built on debt, and electricity bills were collected monthly; after 1929, the Great Depression caused a sharp decline in electricity consumption, but the debt did not shrink accordingly. Technology creates value, but it doesn't guarantee that shareholders will live to see that value realized. The third question: Can the profits remain with the model company long-term? This is a matter of competitive advantage. Why do customers choose Claude? Because it's easy to use. But what if another company is equally good, and cheaper? If customers only access large models via APIs, they can easily switch vendors. If competitors release models with better performance, customers will switch. For example, in September 2026, OpenAI launched GPT-6 Astra. The following week, on the third-party model platform OpenRouter, users spent more money on OpenAI models than on Anthropic. Relying solely on temporary technological advantages, the large model business can easily become a commodity. For example, electricity is a commodity; various power plants produce electricity of similar quality and price. Few people question which power plant produced this particular kilowatt-hour. A true competitive advantage comes only from deep integration with customers. Another detail in the prospectus: Anthropic acknowledges that bottlenecks in enterprise deployment are not only model capabilities, but also inadequate system connectivity, lack of established governance rules, and redesigned workflows. Therefore, the company sends dedicated teams to client organizations to help design and deploy specific applications. The Anthropic prospectus mentions AIG, a large insurance company. AIG's collaboration with Anthropic involves embedding Claude into the underwriting process to jointly build business applications. Previously, underwriters might spend weeks collecting data before starting to compile risk summaries. Now, in already deployed businesses, they can start working from the risk summaries and complete audit trails generated by Claude, focusing their efforts on review and judgment. According to the company, AIG Assist has reduced application review time by more than 90% in its deployed business scope. At this point, customers are not just buying a model response, but also integrating data, revising governance rules, and redeploying employees. When these processes heavily rely on Claude, switching vendors becomes more difficult. However, the moat formed by deep customer ties may not belong to the model company, but also to the application company building on top of the model. For example, WorkBuddy's approach keeps the underlying model replaceable, keeping customers' work on a single platform. The domestic version currently lists built-in models including Hunyuan, DeepSeek, Zhipu, MiniMax, and Kimi, and users can also integrate their purchased third-party model services. The advantage of this is that WorkBuddy can integrate regardless of which model prevails. The model handles understanding and reasoning, while the workbench organizes tools and execution processes. Workbuddy also integrates with WeChat Work, so employees don't need to change their daily work interface; AI can directly participate in the team's collaborative processes of task assignment, deliverables, and review and modification. As a team's data, tool connections, work standards, and collaboration habits gradually converge here, changing the underlying model doesn't necessarily require changing the entire work environment. Competition among model vendors can actually become a condition for the workbench to improve services and control costs. If a customer relies on a specific model, the advantage may remain with the model company; if a customer relies on a workbench that organizes models, data, processes, and tools, the advantage may be concentrated in applications like WorkBuddy. So, is large-scale modeling a good business? Anthropic's prospectus offers a significant improvement over the previous notion that "models only burn money": direct service costs are covered by revenue, gross profit is rapidly improving, and operating cash flow is turning positive. However, it hasn't yet proven that it can reliably retain cash available to shareholders after continuously developing next-generation models and fulfilling its long-term computing power commitments. If I were to boldly predict the future, I believe the ultimate outcome of the large-scale modeling competition will likely see two types of businesses: basic intelligence will increasingly resemble a utility, while cutting-edge intelligence will become more like a "luxury." As technology advances, price competition will intensify as more and more models overcome the capability barriers of everyday tasks. Organizing meeting minutes, categorizing goods, writing a notification, identifying anomalies in spreadsheets—in the real world, much of the work requires accuracy, stability, and affordability, not just intelligence. To accomplish these tasks, there's no reason for companies to pay for the world's smartest model every time. When several models can perform the same task well, customers will naturally start comparing prices. At this point, basic intelligence will increasingly resemble services like water, electricity, and communication: readily available, purchased on demand, with suppliers competing on cost, scale, and service quality. Intelligence becoming infrastructure may mean it's more indispensable, but also harder to sell at a high price. Companies like Anthropic, which pursue "top-tier intelligence," can still be the "LV of the large-scale model world": in a market where basic capabilities are becoming increasingly widespread, they can retain a niche where customers are willing to pay more—continuously delivering better results on complex tasks. Finally, stepping outside the perspective of a single company or industry, from a long-term perspective, the road for AI is still very long. Even now, we are still in the early stages of the intelligent revolution. Anthropic's prospectus also reveals that AI penetration remains very low—while over half of Fortune 500 companies are Anthropic customers with annual spending exceeding $100,000, their average spending on Anthropic is less than 0.1% of their total expenditure, with even the top 10 users accounting for less than 1%. The Anthropic prospectus is also interesting; it doesn't begin with its own performance figures, but with three images: a red bacterial colony, a cross-section of an ammonite, and an ancient celestial map. What does this mean? I believe it represents the vast space waiting to be explored by humankind, from microscopic life to the macroscopic universe. The accompanying text reads: "We believe that AI is one of the most far-reaching technologies in human history. If managed properly, it can rapidly accelerate scientific innovation, significantly increase economic growth rates, make cures for major diseases readily available, and solve problems that have remained unsolved for generations." I also believe in such a vast and promising future. But the road to it is destined to be winding and arduous.
